segments.text: The north-east monsoon is here, and Singapore's wettest months have begun. Almost every afternoon, the sky turns dark and the rain pours down. But where does all this rain come from? And where does it go?

First, last time's question. Why shouldn't you put a greasy food box in the blue recycling bin? Its food and oil dirty the clean paper and plastic around it, so a whole load of recycling might have to be burnt instead. Keep your recycling clean and dry!

Welcome to TheOneApp, Explored! Today, you'll learn three things. First, how water evaporates. Second, how clouds and rain form. And third, how rain finds its way back to our reservoirs. Let's get started!
Are you ready? Three! Two! One! Go!

Here's the news. The north-east monsoon season has begun. From November to January, Singapore gets some of its heaviest rain of the year. And we don't waste it. Drains and canals carry the rain into our reservoirs. About two-thirds of Singapore's land catches rain this way.

Did you feel that journey? You were a tiny water molecule in MacRitchie Reservoir. The Sun's heat made you evaporate into water vapour. You met friends from a puddle, the sea and a river. High in the cold sky, you condensed into a tiny droplet in a cloud. The droplets joined and grew, and fell as rain, which flowed through the drains, all the way home.

Now for the textbook link! In Primary Four, you learn about the water cycle. When water gains heat, it evaporates: it changes from a liquid into a gas called water vapour. When water vapour loses heat, it condenses back into tiny drops of liquid water. Round and round, evaporation and condensation move water all over our planet.
And here's a surprise. When sea water evaporates, the salt stays behind. So rain is fresh water, even when it came from the sea!
Try this at home! After it rains, find a puddle on a sunny path. Draw around its edge with chalk. Come back every hour and draw around it again. Watch it shrink! Where did the water go?
Think about it! Why do wet clothes dry faster on a sunny, windy day than on a cloudy, still day? I'll tell you the answer next time.

So remember. The Sun's heat makes water evaporate. High in the sky, water vapour condenses into clouds. The drops grow, fall as rain, and flow back to our reservoirs. Then it all starts again. Next time: where does your energy come from?
